subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: Hafsa, when I was small we were three children in the house, and every evening the same fight: who laid the table, who swept, who watered the plants. So one Sunday I, Tenzin, took a big sheet of paper. We wrote the chores across the top and our three names down the side, then drew arrows so the names moved one place each week. Pinned on the kitchen door, everyone could see whose turn it was. I liked it because nobody had to say 'You always do less'. The fight faded, though my brother still forgot the plants now and then, and we laughed at that.

qa.q: Where was the chore chart pinned?
qa.a: The chart was pinned on the kitchen door.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the chart in the kitchen?
qa.a: Tenzin liked it because nobody had to argue about who did less, which suggests a feeling of relief and fairness.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped end the fights, and why?
qa.a: Making the names move one place each week helped, because everyone did every chore and the turns were visible.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's brother have seen the chart?
qa.a: Tenzin's brother sometimes forgot the plants, and the group laughed about it, so the chart probably felt fair even when a turn was missed.

grounding: Three siblings write chores on a chart with rotating names so the sharing is open and nobody feels they do more than others.
